rationale:
Quota: 1 long, 3 Shorts, 0 carousels. Every piece is about GLP-1 medicines, and each is a felt symptom or practical moment.

**Long video (L1)**
- The search-demand check is met: at least 4 of the last 7 long videos used a search format (Foundayo What to Expect, Mounjaro vs Ozempic, Zepbound vs Wegovy, Serious Risks). So today can be Lane A.
- Queue items 1 and 2 are already made and only need fixes before publishing, so they aren't planned again here. Item 3, Serious Risks, is a re-render of a held video and still owed. If its re-timed render is ready, the playbook rule to ship the next ready video still applies.
- L1 is therefore queue item 4, "Tirzepatide After 6 Months". It is a fresh, evergreen what-to-expect timeline built on the label, SURMOUNT-1 at 72 weeks and the SURMOUNT-1 three-year (176-week) prediabetes follow-up, all of which are verifiable in depth. It is the next part of the First Month → Months 2–6 series, and it must not repeat Plateau, How Long, Months 2–6 or Weight Loss.

**Radar topics left out**
- ATTAIN-OSA: the Exp I 48-hour window doesn't apply. The result came out in JAMA on 11-09, we covered it in a Short on 11-11, and the playbook says news Shorts underperform.
- The mammogram/breast-density story: it is a small observational conference study marked caution, and the playbook says news and observational studies don't work in Shorts. Retatrutide (pipeline drug) and STEP Young (children, outside our audience) are out for the same kinds of reasons.

**Shorts**
- S1 (08:00): Foundayo plus a practical pill moment ("swallow it whole?"). This follows the double-down on Foundayo by name. It is a new angle: we've already done Foundayo hair, headache, nausea, Thanksgiving and "why a pill can still cause nausea".
- S2 (13:00): a spin-off of L1 on a felt moment, "scale slowing down months in", using SURMOUNT-1's average curve.
- S3 (20:00): the holiday-table slot, which runs through 11-27. Its felt moment, constipation in the days after a big holiday meal, hasn't been used yet in the holiday set; the 11-01 Short was about adding fibre too fast.

**Balance:** no pillar is used more than twice (get-the-most ×2, life-on-glp1, results). Stages: S1 rising (Foundayo by name), S3 peaking (holiday), and the two evergreen pieces have refreshed hooks. Body systems are spread out: GI shows up in S3 only as a main topic.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) after 6 months: what to expect from month 6 onward. The rest of the SURMOUNT-1 average curve to 72 weeks, what the label says about side effects easing, cardiometabolic changes reported at 72 weeks (waist, blood pressure), what the SURMOUNT-1 3-year prediabetes follow-up shows about the longer term, and how attention shifts from losing weight to keeping muscle, labs and results (series part 3)
pieces.angle: Working title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) After 6 Months: What the Big Trial Showed'. Opening: 'Six months into tirzepatide? In the big obesity trial, average weight loss kept going but slowed, and the focus shifts to keeping your results.' Chapter 2 title: 'Does the nausea keep easing?' Quote the label sentence exactly: 'The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time.' Cite the label edition actually used (DailyMed shows a 16 Nov 2026 revision). Chapter 4: frame the 3-year results as trial averages in adults with prediabetes plus obesity or overweight, and say that preventing diabetes is not an approved use. Everything else stays as briefed.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) After 6 Months: What to Expect?
pieces.why:
Playbook queue item 4 and series part 3. A searched what-to-expect format resting on settled label and SURMOUNT-1 evidence, with steady search and a New Year spike to come. | fact-check: Good evergreen topic: series part 3, a clear search question and strong evidence. These parts check out: the SURMOUNT-1 72-week results (Jastreboff, NEJM 2022) and the 3-year prediabetes analysis (Lancet, 176 weeks: 1.3% vs 13.3% developed type 2 diabetes, then 2.4% vs 13.7% after 17 weeks off treatment). Four fixes before scripting.
(1) The side-effect wording in the brief is wrong. The current Zepbound label on DailyMed (revised 16 Nov 2026, newer than the 28 Aug 2026 date in our notes) says: "The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time." Copy that sentence exactly. It only covers nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, so chapter 2 can't say side effects in general ease. Don't write 'mostly', and don't apply the sentence to constipation, hair loss or anything else. Cite the label edition the script actually uses, with its real revision date. Re-check the Table 2 numbers in that edition, because the hair-loss figure may have changed.
(2) Brand scope. SURMOUNT-1 is the obesity trial (adults without diabetes), which matches Zepbound's approved use. Mounjaro is approved for type 2 diabetes. A title that names only Mounjaro mislabels the data.
(3) Wording in the opening. 'Keeping what you've gained' is confusing in a weight-loss video. Use 'keeping your results'.
(4) The prediabetes chapter must say these are trial averages in people with prediabetes plus obesity or overweight, that preventing diabetes is not an approved use, and that 'developed type 2 diabetes' is the trial's measure. Never call it 'prevents diabetes'.
Keep the full DXA scope (160-person substudy, about 75% fat and 25% lean, lean mass isn't pure muscle), the kidney caveat on protein, and the line about never changing blood pressure medicines on your own. Before scripting, check the live list for overlap with Months 2–6, Plateau and How Long.

pieces.topic: Orforglipron (Foundayo) pill: can you split, crush or chew it? What the US label says about swallowing the tablet whole
pieces.angle:
08:00 practical 'Is this OK?' moment. Follow the task's length arm and hook archetype.
- Sentence 1 (14 words or fewer) names Foundayo and gives the answer, e.g. 'Foundayo, the orforglipron pill: the US label says swallow it whole.' Scene 1's on-screen text matches it.
- By 6 s: the label's administration wording, copied from Foundayo PI rev 7/2026 section 2: once daily, with or without food, swallow tablets whole. Add 'any time of day' only if the PI prints it. Don't explain why unless the label says why.
- Untagged lines: 'Trouble swallowing pills? Ask your pharmacist or prescriber, not a kitchen knife.' Don't split or crush on your own.
- One label GI line: nausea is common, higher during dose escalation, and decreased over time (Foundayo wording).
- No dose numbers or schedules, and no comparison with other pills.
- Close with the fixed don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and a loop to sentence 1. No subscribe or link line. 160 words or fewer.
- Post note (Exp G): target is the Foundayo long video (LWyUfli67CI), switching to the new Foundayo What to Expect video once it's live.
pieces.working_title: Foundayo (Orforglipron) Pill: Can You Split or Crush It? #shorts
pieces.why: Foundayo by name with a practical moment is our strongest Short signal (897 and 841 views). This angle is new: hair, headache, nausea and Thanksgiving are already done.

pieces.topic: Months into tirzepatide and the scale is moving slower: what SURMOUNT-1's average curve shows about weight loss slowing over time
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro): Scale Slowing Months In? #shorts'. Sentence 1: 'Tirzepatide and the scale slowing months in? In the big trial, average loss slowed too.' Then: averages aren't predictions, so look at the trend and other measures with your prescriber. Every number comes from L1's verified script. Everything else as briefed.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Scale Slowing Down Months In? #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. A felt progress moment that sends traffic into the after-6-months long video and the first-months series. | fact-check: The evidence is fine: in SURMOUNT-1 the average curve fell fastest early and flattened toward 72 weeks. Two risks. (1) The 'relief' framing could suggest that any one person's slowdown is normal or expected. Keep it to trial averages, and say plainly that only a prescriber can judge an individual's progress. (2) The brand in the title. SURMOUNT-1 tested adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, which is Zepbound's approved use, not Mounjaro's. Every number must match L1's verified script exactly, so this Short can't be finalised until L1 passes its content check. Use no figure values that aren't marked 'about', and no week where the curve 'plateaus' unless the NEJM paper states it.

pieces.topic: Backed up in the days after a big holiday dinner on tirzepatide: how often the label reports constipation vs placebo, and gentle next-day habits
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) and Constipation: What the Label Says #shorts'. Sentence 1: 'Tirzepatide and feeling backed up over the holidays? Constipation is on the label.' Stat card: constipation was about 11 to 17% on Zepbound vs 5% on placebo over 72 weeks, with the population copied exactly from the Table 2 heading. Next, as its own label line with no 'so': tirzepatide delays gastric emptying. Two tips: sip fluids through the day unless you've been told to limit fluids, and take a gentle walk. Ask a pharmacist before any laxative. Then the Medication Guide red flag word for word, the fixed don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro): Backed Up After the Holiday Dinner? #shorts
pieces.why: Holiday felt-symptom Shorts work (491, 320 and 263 views), and this morning-after GI moment hasn't been used in this year's holiday set. It feeds the Thanksgiving long video. | fact-check: A useful topic, but the label facts in the brief are off and the title invents a cause. (1) Table 2 in the current Zepbound label (DailyMed, revised 16 Nov 2026) gives constipation at week 72 as 17% (5 mg), 14% (10 mg) and 11% (15 mg) vs 5% for placebo, not 6%. 'Top dose vs placebo' (11% vs 5%) also picks the lowest rate. Give the range instead, with no dose numbers: 'about 11 to 17% vs 5% on placebo'. (2) The table pools Studies 1 and 2, and Study 2 enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes. Copy the population exactly as the table's heading states it, not the obesity-only wording in the brief. Cite the edition actually used with its real revision date (the 28 Aug 2026 date in our notes looks out of date). (3) The label doesn't tie constipation to big meals or holidays. The title and hook 'Backed up after the holiday dinner?' imply that the dinner causes it, which is the same cause-and-timing fault flagged on S3 11-23. Make the holiday the setting, not the cause. (4) The gastric emptying sentence must stand alone, with no 'so' and no link to constipation. (5) The red flag must copy the Medication Guide's patient wording: severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without vomiting → stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away. Name no laxative products, and keep 'unless you've been told to limit fluids'.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs dulaglutide (Trulicity) in the SURPASS-CVOT randomized head-to-head trial (NEJM 2025): adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, about 13,000 people, followed for about 4 years. Covers the main heart-outcome result (heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death), what 'non-inferior' means, death from any cause, A1C and weight, stomach side effects and stopping rates, and questions for your prescriber.
pieces.angle: Mounjaro vs Trulicity (SURPASS-CVOT, NEJM 2025, PMID 41406444), in adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic CVD only. Sentence 1: 'If you have type 2 diabetes and heart disease: in a trial that randomly assigned about thirteen thousand adults to tirzepatide or dulaglutide for about four years, heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths were slightly less frequent on tirzepatide, about twelve in every hundred people compared with about thirteen on dulaglutide. That met the bar for being no worse, but it was not shown to be better.' On-screen stat: 12.2% vs 13.1%, HR 0.92 (95.3% CI 0.83–1.01), non-inferior; superiority not shown. Death from any cause: secondary outcome, reported exactly with the paper's HR/CI and hedging ('lower in this trial'). Chapter 6: quote the live Mounjaro PI section 1 CV-risk indication (approved 28 Aug 2026; confirm the revision date on DailyMed) word for word. Say its population ('adults with type 2 diabetes at high risk for cardiovascular events') is broader than the trial's, and that this is not a reason to switch medicines. Quote the Trulicity PI CV indication verbatim at its own URL. Keep all safety and prescriber lines as briefed. Avoid Lilly marketing phrasing and post hoc and imputed-placebo analyses.
pieces.working_title: Mounjaro vs Trulicity: Which Protected the Heart More?
pieces.why:
Approved-drug head-to-head against tirzepatide, our best-performing search-demand format, built on one peer-reviewed RCT plus the labels. It's easy to verify, it isn't a repeat (different trial from SURPASS-2 and SURMOUNT-5), and it replaces the held L1. | fact-check: The topic is sound, safe and on-pillar (beyond-weight, type 2 diabetes). I checked these facts: SURPASS-CVOT is real. Nicholls et al., 'Cardiovascular Outcomes with Tirzepatide versus Dulaglutide in Type 2 Diabetes', N Engl J Med 2025 Dec 18;393(24):2409-2420, PMID 41406444 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41406444/). 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic CVD were randomized (6,586 to tirzepatide and 6,579 to dulaglutide in the analysed sets) and followed for a median of about 4 years. The primary outcome (CV death, heart attack or stroke) happened in 12.2% on tirzepatide vs 13.1% on dulaglutide: HR 0.92, 95.3% CI 0.83 to 1.01, P=0.003 for non-inferiority, P=0.09 for superiority. So it is non-inferior and superiority was not shown. Secondary results reported in coverage: death from any cause HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.94). GI adverse events were more common on tirzepatide (about 42.5% vs 35.9% in secondary reports; take the exact per-arm figures from the NEJM paper itself).

The brief needs four changes:
(1) The example sentence 1 says 'similar or somewhat lower on tirzepatide'. Because the CI crosses 1 and superiority was not shown, 'somewhat lower' overstates the result. Use 'slightly fewer on tirzepatide (about twelve vs thirteen in every hundred), but not enough to show it was better'.
(2) Label status has changed. The FDA approved a Mounjaro indication on 28 Aug 2026 to lower the risk of MACE (CV death, non-fatal heart attack or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes at high risk for CV events. So chapter 6 should quote the live Mounjaro PI section 1 wording exactly from DailyMed. That label population ('high risk for CV events') is wider than the trial's (established ASCVD), so keep the two clearly separate and don't generalize the trial result.
(3) Death from any cause is a secondary outcome. Report the HR and CI as the paper does, with its hedging. Don't call it proof that tirzepatide 'saves lives', and don't present it as a formally confirmed superiority result unless the NEJM paper says so.
(4) Don't use Lilly promotional phrases ('first and only… proven to lower') or the Diabetes Care imputed-placebo analysis (PMID 41940793) as if they were trial results. The JAMA Cardiology cardiorenal post hoc (PMID 41903177) and the Lancet D&E kidney analysis are out of scope, unless one line labels them exploratory.

Everything else in the brief (scope locks, safety lines, no dosing or switching, the Trulicity PI CV wording at its own URL, the Lilly funding line) is appropriate.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) and fatty liver: what MASLD and MASH are, how excess weight and insulin resistance are linked to liver fat, what the randomized SYNERGY-NASH Phase 2 trial found on liver biopsy, what the SURPASS-3 MRI substudy found about liver fat in type 2 diabetes, and why fatty liver isn't an approved use for tirzepatide
pieces.angle: Keep the brief as written, with these changes. 1) Opening sentence 1: 'If you've been told you have a fatty liver and you're wondering whether tirzepatide helps: in one randomized Phase 2 trial in adults with MASH and moderate or advanced liver scarring, more people on tirzepatide than on placebo had their MASH resolve on a liver biopsy after fifty-two weeks. It isn't an approved use, so it's one to talk through with your doctor.' 2) Primary result: 10% on placebo vs 44%, 56% and 62% on the lowest, middle and highest tirzepatide doses tested. Say no mg values on screen or in narration. The per-arm n comes from the NEJM paper. Fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of MASH was a secondary outcome: 30% vs 55%, 51% and 51%. Never describe MASH resolution as 'inflammation went away'. 3) SURPASS-3 MRI: present it as a separate substudy in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor. It measured liver fat content by MRI over 52 weeks, comparing the two higher tirzepatide arms pooled vs insulin degludec. Use the absolute percentage-point change exactly as the PubMed abstract gives it, and don't present it as resolution or fibrosis data. 4) Approval chapter: quote Section 1 of the live Mounjaro PI (including the major adverse cardiovascular events indication if it appears on the live label) and of the live Zepbound PI (including obstructive sleep apnea). Read the revised dates on DailyMed. Credit FDA in one neutral line: semaglutide (Wegovy) is approved in the US for adults with noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. No comparison, no ranking, no switching. 5) Keep all safety lines, the 'recommended, not proven on tirzepatide' framing for lifestyle habits, and the hepatologist question list. Thumbnail 'LIVER FAT?' with one calm, fully drawn, labelled character, no organ imagery and no body-shaming. Verified sources so far: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38856224/.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) and Fatty Liver: Does It Help?
pieces.why: Fills today's dropped long-video slot with a topic the channel hasn't covered. It rests on settled randomized evidence (NEJM SYNERGY-NASH, SURPASS-3 MRI) plus label Section 1, so it can pass the fact-check first time, and drug-name searches ('Mounjaro fatty liver') keep bringing in viewers over time. | fact-check: The topic is sound, fits the channel and has strong evidence behind it. I checked these points: (1) SYNERGY-NASH (Loomba et al., NEJM 2024; PubMed 38856224, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38856224/) was a Phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding trial. It enrolled 190 adults with biopsy-confirmed noncirrhotic MASH and stage F2–F3 fibrosis, treated for 52 weeks. MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis was 10% on placebo vs 44%, 56% and 62% across the three tirzepatide arms. Improvement of at least one fibrosis stage without worsening of MASH was a secondary endpoint: 30% vs 55%, 51% and 51%. (2) Tirzepatide still has no US approval for MASLD or MASH. Its approved uses are type 2 diabetes (Mounjaro, which also has a 2026 approval to lower major cardiovascular event risk in type 2 diabetes), chronic weight management (Zepbound) and moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity (Zepbound). (3) FDA approved semaglutide (Wegovy) in August 2025 for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis (F2–F3). Fixes needed: (a) The sample opening says 'liver inflammation resolve'. That is inaccurate: MASH resolution on biopsy is a composite histology endpoint, not just inflammation. (b) The angle asks for per-arm results but also bans dose numbers. Keep the ban and describe the arms without milligrams. (c) In SURPASS-3 MRI (Gastaldelli et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2022), the primary liver-fat comparison pooled two tirzepatide arms against insulin degludec. Say so, and report the result as a change in liver fat content measured by MRI-PDFF, not 'fatty liver resolved'. Confirm the exact figures on PubMed before scripting. (d) The FDA line for Wegovy must keep 'noncirrhotic' and 'moderate to advanced fibrosis' and say it is used alongside diet and exercise, as FDA prints it. (e) The SURPASS-CVOT approval may be missing from older label text. Quote Section 1 from the live Mounjaro PI and the live Zepbound PI on DailyMed and use their actual revised dates. Everything else in the angle (no 'reverses' or 'cures', guideline habits marked 'recommended', a clinician line, the pancreatitis emergency wording, the low-blood-sugar caveat) is correct; keep it. I found no misinformation or strike risk once these fixes are in.

pieces.topic: Zepbound (tirzepatide) single-dose vial vs single-dose pen: what's in the box, what each device asks you to do, storage, injection sites and disposal, taken only from the US prescribing information and each device's own Instructions for Use
pieces.angle:
A side-by-side device how-to, 9–11 min.

**Gate:** script it only if the Lilly Zepbound single-dose vial IFU and single-dose pen IFU both load at their own URLs with readable revised dates. Read the Zepbound PI date on DailyMed (sections 2, 3, 16 and 17 only). If the vial IFU doesn't load, drop L4 and ship the next ready video in the queue.

**Opening:** sentence 1 names Zepbound and answers the question. Something like: 'If your Zepbound comes as a vial instead of a pen, it's the same medicine, tirzepatide, but you use a separate syringe and needle, and the vial's instructions add steps the pen does for you.' The second payoff at 15–30 s is the first concrete vial step from the vial IFU. Say early that KwikPens have their own leaflet: follow the one in your box and ask a pharmacist to show you.

**Chapters, named as the questions people search:**
1. What's in the box with each one? Only what each IFU lists.
2. What does the pen do that the vial doesn't? Pen steps from the pen IFU (unlock, place flat, press, the clicks, hold).
3. Using the vial: the steps in vial-IFU wording (supplies, wiping the stopper, the syringe steps). Never speak or show syringe markings, amounts or doses. Say the vial is single-dose only if the IFU says so, and quote its line about leftover medicine exactly.
4. Where to inject and rotating sites, in PI or IFU wording.
5. Storage and time out of the fridge, with the exact limits from PI section 16 and each IFU.
6. Disposal: the IFU wording plus the FDA sharps guidance, 'follow your local rules', and never loose sharps in household trash.
7. When to call: injection-site reactions at 6–8% by dose vs about 2% on placebo (PI 6.1, with the population on the card), the full allergy emergency card, then the fixed don't-stop line.

**Rules:**
- No cost, coverage, Medicare, switching or 'which is better' talk.
- No technique beyond the IFUs, and no dose, missed-dose or titration content.
- Re-hook every 45–75 s. Land the last new fact before 80%, and keep lists to 3 items at most.
- One subscribe ask, after the chapter 3 payoff.
- 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line are spoken and shown on screen.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' The publisher links the pen how-to video (qiLPt1hHGL0).
- Thumbnail: 'VIAL OR PEN?' with one calm labelled character holding both devices. No body imagery.
pieces.working_title: Zepbound (Tirzepatide) Vial vs Pen: What's Different?
pieces.why: A queued search-demand device how-to built on primary label and IFU sources, so it should pass the fact-check first time. It doesn't repeat the dropped topics or today's Shorts, and it gives the pen and injection Shorts a new link target.
